Individual contextual follow-up, November 17–22, 2026. The marker spans the page break between supplied PDF pp. 43–44 and concerns the balance between technological development and foundational science. Stone’s original report was read at its definitions, methodological caveats and funding discussion. It argues that development is favored over basic and applied research and documents the distinction between these categories; it does not show that China has no foundational scientific activity. Its p. 14 expressly rejects an innate distinctiveness in individual Chinese scientific inquiry and warns about interpreting headline indicators. The citing report supplies no year, denominator or threshold for little foundational science. The structural-policy criticism is supported as Stone’s analysis, while the broad magnitude and any extension to present conditions remain unverified. This audit does not infer research theft from spending categories. Stone’s returnee-impact discussion is on p. 18 in the recovered source, not the cited p. 12. Its underlying Cao, Baas, Wagner and Jonkers study was traced to the authors’ October 2019 preprint, identified separately from the 2020 published journal version. Its methods and Figure 4 compare publication-based mobility cohorts and citation impact. A first publication in China followed by a foreign affiliation is a mobility proxy, not a direct measure of where someone was educated; the authors explicitly note missing people who left before their first indexed publication. Higher cohort citation impact does not establish that overseas education caused it or that China lacks a scientific base. The report’s Western-trained/domestically-produced wording therefore overstates what was measured. The publication-page/edition mismatch and access gap to the exact final journal version remain explicit. The historian attribution was traced beyond Stone to Zhang Jian’s original 2010 article, reproduced in full by Renmin University with the matching journal, issue and pp. 27–45. Zhang analyzes an evolving modern historical movement, including its eventual turn toward autonomous truth-seeking science; his argument is more qualified than a timeless claim that Chinese science is merely technology. Stone’s paraphrase appears on p. 19 in the recovered edition, not the cited p. 13. Visual inspection also confirms an internal citation error: the Zhang sentence points to endnote 45, which is Ibid after Vannevar Bush, while the actual Zhang article is listed at note 41. The correct originating work is now linked as evidence, preserving the intermediary’s error rather than propagating it. The unlocated earlier edition is not assumed identical. This is a separate and stronger inference: that China can acquire or build technology but lacks the accompanying scientific base. The cited Stone p. 15 in the recovered original is an organization-of-report page, not evidence for that conclusion. Elsewhere Stone discusses funding and governance weaknesses, while the originating bibliometric study documents growing Chinese science and contributions by returnees. Neither establishes a categorical absence of foundational knowledge, nor does either identify a particular stolen technology and measure its associated knowledge deficit. The inference needs explicit definitions, dates and case evidence. It remains unresolved rather than being certified by the preceding historian quotation or a comparative citation-impact result.

The target is industry scale above RMB 400 billion, not exactly RMB 400 billion. Its 60-percent domestic-application contribution measure includes BeiDou and compatible products; the 80-percent target is above that level in important applications. Those denominators should not be silently restated as ordinary BeiDou-only sales market shares. These are policy targets, not measured 2020 outcomes. The shorthand reference is linked to the already indexed full original, preserving its old row. The document identification on supplied PDF p. 37 matches the original General Office of the State Council notice, document 97 of 2013. Its signed date is September 26 and publication date October 9; both dates in the citation chain are explicable. The plan contains the dated industry goals described next. Calling it the most important document is the report’s qualified assessment, not a formally ranked legal status established by the notice. The live record’s inactive label is retained as a present access-state observation, not projected back onto the report’s historical discussion. The original State Council General Office instrument, 2013 No. 97, was read in its opening rationale. It supports the attributed policy argument about productivity, living standards and national competitiveness. The report’s commercial-efficiency wording is a looser English rendering of social production efficiency, not a verbatim English original. Signature September 26, 2013 and publication October 9 are both displayed. The live record now labels this historical plan no longer effective, so it must not be presented as the current operative rulebook. The narrow finding is an accurately attributed historical policy rationale, not proof that the promised economic effects occurred. Adjacent 2020/2035 statements have other notes. The organizational-policy claim on supplied PDF p. 40 cites the same 2013 plan. Section II(3) and the innovation-policy provisions call for strengthening institutional platforms and industry clustering. This corroborates policy support for the categories of research organization described. It does not establish that the plan first created the entire organizational system or that each institution was newly founded in 2013. That causal founding chronology needs dated establishment records. This check concerns public institutional policy only, without assessing chip engineering, technical research methods or a current military production network. The exclusivity claim on supplied PDF p. 39 exceeds the cited 2013 plan. Its section II(3) calls for comprehensive application of BeiDou and other satellite-navigation systems in electricity, finance and communications; the Chinese wording 北斗等 does not require BeiDou to be the sole system. The plan also explicitly promotes compatibility and interoperability. The report’s inferred desire to reduce GPS dependence should therefore be separated from a purported exclusive-use mandate. The same source was read once for these different claims, with the shorthand link restored and original record retained.

The complete compound note includes Ge’s commentary, the CNA study and two distinct strategy books; both omitted book associations are restored. The original RTI economic study was checked at PDF pp. 223–224, including printed Table 14-2 on p. 14-3. Its opening strategic-interest, commanding-height and international-status propositions are present. The ending requires translation reconciliation: the available CASI text describes a political issue involving long-term stability and a strategic issue in the information and intelligent ages, whereas the report quotes economic position and robotic age. These are not silently treated as identical verbatim wording; an original Chinese facsimile or the authors’ translation basis is needed to settle the rendering. The report renders the term as coercion; that translation choice should remain explicit rather than implying identical English editions.
